114	## Overrides Pattern
115	
116	All customizations live in `overrides/` mirroring the structure of `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/`. Never edit `node_modules/`.
117	
118	**Minimise custom code.** When implementing Zimmermann's design and layout, stay as close to the base PWA Kit implementation as possible. Style changes (CSS, Chakra props, theme tokens) are always expected and need no confirmation. 120	**Before any change:** check whether the file exists in `overrides/`. If not, create the override:

122	1. Copy from `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/` to the mirrored path in `overrides/`.

160	## Contentful Content Type Management
161	
162	Content types (schema) are never created manually in the Contentful web app. They are defined in code and synced via a script. This makes schema changes reviewable, repeatable, and team-safe.
163	
164	**Key paths:**
165	
166	- `scripts/contentful/sync.js` — runner: upserts (creates or updates) and publishes every content type in the definitions directory
167	- `scripts/contentful/content-types/` — one `.js` file per content type (e.g. `shoppableImage.js`)
168	
169	**To register a new content type:**
170	
171	1. Add a definition file to `scripts/contentful/content-types/<contentTypeId>.js` (see existing files for shape)
172	2. Run `npm run sync:contentful`
173	
174	**To run the sync:**
175	
176	```
177	npm run sync:contentful
178	```
179	
180	Requires `CONTENTFUL_MANAGEMENT_TOKEN` — a personal token tied to your own Contentful account — in `.env.shared` (never commit; run `npm run env -- init` to scaffold it, then `npm run env -- <tier>` to activate a tier before running the sync). 182	The script is idempotent — safe to re-run. It preserves any existing fields not in the definition file (it will not delete fields from a live content type).

260	
261	The SSR layer in `overrides/app/ssr.js` uses **Node's native `fetch`**, which is backed by `undici`. 263	```ts
264	import { Pool } from 'undici';
265	
266	// 1. Create isolated pools for specific origins
267	const checkoutPool = new Pool('https://api.checkout-service.com', {
268	  connections: 10, // Hard limit of 10 concurrent connections to this origin
269	  timeout: 8000,
270	});
271	
272	// 2. Use them explicitly in your fetch calls inside ssr.js
273	async function getCheckoutMetadata() {
274	  return await fetch('https://api.checkout-service.com/v1/metadata', {
275	    dispatcher: checkoutPool, // Safely isolated!
276	  });
277	}
278	```

# Architecture

_Key technical decisions, stack overview, overrides pattern, component organisation, and key paths. Update this file when the stack changes, a new integration is added, or a structural decision is made._

Production storefront for www.zimmermann.com — multi-locale, multi-currency, eight storefronts across six regions (AU, US, UK, EU, HK, ME), with both EU and US each split into two storefronts (domestic + international).

## Pre-Build Decisions

These decisions affect tooling, CI, and code shape that's hard to retrofit later. Status as of 2026-05-29.

| #   | Decision                     | Status                                 |
| --- | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| 1   | Browser & device matrix      | ✅ Confirmed (informal)                |
| 2   | Accessibility manual testing | 🟡 Partial — vendor info pending       |
| 3   | Performance budgets          | ✅ Confirmed (informal)                |
| 4   | Client-side error reporting  | ⚪ Accepted risk — no tool             |
| 5   | Feature-flag tool            | ⚪ Accepted risk — Optimizely Web only |
| 6   | Translation fallback chain   | 🟡 Partial — Brand/Legal pending       |

### #1 — Browser & device matrix ✅

**Mobile perf-test floor:** current OS version −2 on iPhone and Android (iOS 17+, Android 14+), verified via BrowserStack Automate. `package.json` browserslist aligned to match.
**Desktop matrix** ([.browserstack.yml](../../.browserstack.yml)): Chrome + Safari (macOS Sonoma), Firefox + Edge (Windows 11) — all latest.

### #2 — Accessibility 🟡

**Target:** WCAG 2.2 AA, at least 2.1 AA. **Automated:** axe-core in Vitest + Playwright; Storybook a11y addon; Lighthouse CI a11y ≥0.90 ([lighthouserc.js](../../lighthouserc.js)). **Manual:** client's existing a11y vendor.
**Pending:** vendor name, screen-reader/browser matrix, audit cadence, remediation owner.

### #3 — Performance budgets ✅

**Client-mandated:** **LCP ≤ 2s** at p75 mobile, plus Lighthouse Performance ≥ 0.80, Accessibility ≥ 0.90, Best Practices ≥ 0.90. These are the only performance numbers in the signed TSD (§9).
**Other CWV (internal working defaults, not client-mandated):** INP ≤ 200ms · CLS ≤ 0.1. Lighthouse mobile defaults at p75.
**CI gate (SIT gate):** Lighthouse CI (`@lhci/cli`) asserts the Lighthouse score floors above, plus a >5pt trend-drop gate (LHCI server required). SEO intentionally not asserted. Runs on every PR to `develop` ([`digital-sit.yml`](../../.github/workflows/digital-sit.yml)), deploys to the **Dev** tier on merge — treat its numbers as a **regression indicator**, not the contractual measurement.
**Contractual measurement:** Client-mandated LCP and Lighthouse numbers are validated on **Stage** — the prod-mimicking tier (same MRT bundle size class, same CDN/edge configuration, same SFCC realm tier as production). The Dev tier is slower and further from the edge, so its absolute numbers will be worse — that is expected and not a sign-off concern. Full environment topology in [tsd-architecture.md §14.1](./temp/tsd-architecture.md).
**Bundle ceilings — internal CI policy, NOT client requirements:** `main.js` 180 kB · `vendor.js` 250 kB · `main.css` 50 kB (`bundlesize` in `package.json`). (These were set as aspirational targets early in the project. As of the last measurement the actual sizes are well above these ceilings (`main.js` ~352 kB, `vendor.js` ~2 MB) before any optimisation pass — the ceilings need to be re-baselined against measured size + a growth-only headroom (e.g. current + 10–15%) once a baseline pass is done.) Their purpose is regression detection, not a client-facing commitment.
**Third-party script weight:** uncapped — tight LCP is the de-facto constraint. See AGENTS.md > Performance for the deferral rule.

### #6 — Translation fallback 🟡

[regional.md](./prd/regional.md) REG-046: "English is the site-wide fallback." Doesn't disambiguate `en-eu` vs `en`, nor split by content type.
**Pending Brand/Legal decision** on the rule per content type:

| Content type | Suggested chain          | Why                                          |
| ------------ | ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------- |
| UI strings   | `fr-eu` → `en-eu` → `en` | Universal meaning                            |
| Editorial    | `fr-eu` → `en-eu` → hide | Avoid half-translated pages                  |
| Product copy | `fr-eu` → `en-eu` → hide | Care/sizing are region-specific (regulatory) |

REG-047 (Contentful↔Transperfect↔SFCC workflow) remains separately TBC.

### Accepted risks

**#4 — No client-side error reporting.** JS errors in customer browsers (e.g. Adyen iframe failure on a specific iOS Safari version) are invisible to the team; detection relies on support tickets. Revisit post-launch if checkout completion dips unexplained.

**#5 — No feature-flag tool.** Optimizely Web Experimentation ([analytics.md](./prd/analytics.md) AAB-004) covers analytics A/B. Note (confirmed 09-06): Optimizely is **not** a GTM tag — the PWA loads its script directly in the page head (US storefront only, single snippet across environments, before render to avoid flicker), Didomi-gated. Progressive rollout, social login dark-launch, and August-2026 payment-method gating will be handled via deploy timing and branch merges — no instant kill-switch, no % rollouts.

## Frontend Stack

### Bundled by PWA Kit

| UI framework                 | React 18 + Chakra UI                                  | Component library + theme system                                                      |
| Routing                      | React Router v6                                       |                                                                                       |
| Server/async state           | TanStack Query (via `@salesforce/commerce-sdk-react`) | All SFCC data fetching                                                                |
| i18n                         | react-intl                                            | Translations in `translations/`                                                       |
| Build + dev server           | Webpack 5 (via `pwa-kit-dev`)                         |                                                                                       |
| Build + test runner (legacy) | Jest (via `pwa-kit-dev test`)                         | `jest.config.js` — kept for PWA Kit internals; superseded by Vitest for project tests |

### Project additions

| Layer                                  | Library                                        | Notes                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Type safety                            | TypeScript strict mode                         | `tsconfig.json`                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Component explorer + interaction tests | Storybook 8                                    | `storybook dev -p 6006`; `play` functions are the primary tool for component-level interaction testing                                                                                                              |
| Storybook a11y addon                   | `@storybook/addon-a11y`                        | Component-level accessibility checks during development and in Storybook test runs                                                                                                                                  |
| Unit test runner                       | Vitest                                         | `vitest.config.ts`; replaces `pwa-kit-dev test` for project tests                                                                                                                                                   |
| Accessibility testing                  | axe-core (via `vitest-axe` / `axe-playwright`) | Automated WCAG checks in unit and E2E layers; see Pre-Build Decisions #2 for outstanding items                                                                                                                      |
| E2E tests (planned)                    | Playwright                                     | Not yet configured                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Forms + validation                     | react-hook-form + zod                          | Not yet installed; add when checkout/account work begins                                                                                                                                                            |
| Global UI state                        | Zustand                                        | For shared state that outgrows Context (multi-step flows, drawer state, etc.). **SSR note:** initialise store per-request — never as a module singleton — to prevent state leaking across server-rendered requests. |

### External services

Salesforce Commerce Cloud, Contentful Studio CMS, Global-e (international checkout + server-side pricing/catalogue feed — PRC-34..43 sign-off pending), Didomi (consent), GTM hosted on Addingwell (data layer + downstream tag loading via Tell No Lies). Full integration map below.

## Environments

Six-tier topology spans **Local → Dev → SIT → UAT → Stage → Prod**. Each tier (other than Local) has its own SFCC realm, Contentful environment, and MuleSoft connections. Ownership splits across three zones — Digital, IT/NewStore, and Shared (Digital + Business).

| #   | Tier            | Owner         | Purpose                                                                      | Third-party availability                                              | Deploy trigger                                                              |
| --- | --------------- | ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | **Local**       | Digital       | Feature build on developer machines                                          | All services mocked (MSW stubs)                                       | `npm start`                                                                 |
| 2   | **Dev**         | Digital       | Integrated digital testing across all 6 storefronts, independent of NewStore | MuleSoft STG · NewStore Dev · Omneo STG · Narvar stub · Adyen sandbox | Merge to `develop`                                                          |
| 3   | **SIT**         | IT / NewStore | NewStore SIT and regression on its own cadence                               | NewStore STG · MuleSoft STG · Narvar STG · AP21 test                  | NewStore release cadence (parallel lane, non-blocking for Digital releases) |
| 4   | **UAT**         | Shared        | Business acceptance across all 6 regions                                     | NewStore STG · Narvar STG · Omneo STG · Adyen sandbox                 | Business approval gate                                                      |
| 5   | **Stage** (E2E) | Shared        | End-to-end testing with all third parties live; time-boxed booked windows    | NewStore STG · MuleSoft STG · Omneo STG · Narvar STG · Adyen sandbox  | Booked 2-week window                                                        |
| 6   | **Prod**        | Live          | Production; AU canary then flag-flip to remaining regions                    | NewStore PROD · MuleSoft PROD · Omneo PROD · Narvar PROD · Adyen PROD | Release manager + canary gate                                               |

**Stage** is the contractual performance-test environment referenced under [Pre-Build Decisions #3](#3--performance-budgets-) — it mirrors production infrastructure (same MRT bundle class, CDN/edge configuration, SFCC realm tier).

**QA workflow** ([`qa.yml`](../.github/workflows/qa.yml)) runs on every PR to `develop` and `release/**`: Vitest unit tests and Storybook interaction + `@storybook/addon-a11y` component-level accessibility checks (`storybook test --ci`), in parallel. Code-correctness checks that run before any environment is involved.

**SIT gate** ([`digital-sit.yml`](../.github/workflows/digital-sit.yml)) runs on push/PR to `release/**`: Playwright `p0` specs, bundle-size check, MuleSoft contract tests, Lighthouse CI thresholds, LHCI trend gate. Environment-dependent checks against the deployed Dev tier. On merge to `develop` it also deploys to Dev. Production deploys are gated on a clean SIT gate run plus stakeholder approval through UAT and Stage.

**MRT targets** in [mobify.config.js](../mobify.config.js) map one-to-one to the topology: `dev | sit | uat | stage | production`. `ENVIRONMENT_NAME` (`local | dev | sit | uat | stage | prod`) is the per-tier tag emitted to Sentry, New Relic, and GTM.

## SSR Requirement (DMU-030)

Server-side rendering is **mandatory** for product, category, and content pages (DMU-030, signed off). PWA Kit's SSR pipeline must be preserved — do not introduce client-only patterns (e.g. `typeof window !== 'undefined'` short-circuits, client-only data fetching on first paint, or `next/dynamic`-style `{ ssr: false }`) on these page types. Any componentry that cannot render on the server must be gated behind a hydration-safe boundary that still emits SEO-relevant markup on the server.

## Overrides Pattern

All customizations live in `overrides/` mirroring the structure of `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/`. Never edit `node_modules/`.

**Minimise custom code.** When implementing Zimmermann's design and layout, stay as close to the base PWA Kit implementation as possible. Style changes (CSS, Chakra props, theme tokens) are always expected and need no confirmation. Structural changes — restructuring components, altering data flow, or significantly deviating from base template behaviour — must be confirmed with the user before proceeding.

**Before any change:** check whether the file exists in `overrides/`. If not, create the override:

1. Copy from `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/` to the mirrored path in `overrides/`.
2. Rename `.js`/`.jsx` → `.ts`/`.tsx`. Replace `PropTypes` with TypeScript `type` definitions. Add explicit types to all parameters, return values, and props. Use Commerce SDK types (`commerce-sdk-isomorphic`, `@salesforce/commerce-sdk-react`) where available. No `as any` or `// @ts-ignore`.
3. Verify `npx tsc --noEmit` passes with zero errors.
4. **Stop. Present the converted file to the user and wait for approval before making any functional changes.**

## New vs. Override Components

- **Overriding a base template component:** copy from `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/` to the mirrored path in `overrides/` (see Overrides Pattern above).

## Contentful Content Type Management

Content types (schema) are never created manually in the Contentful web app. They are defined in code and synced via a script. This makes schema changes reviewable, repeatable, and team-safe.

**Key paths:**

- `scripts/contentful/sync.js` — runner: upserts (creates or updates) and publishes every content type in the definitions directory
- `scripts/contentful/content-types/` — one `.js` file per content type (e.g. `shoppableImage.js`)

**To register a new content type:**

1. Add a definition file to `scripts/contentful/content-types/<contentTypeId>.js` (see existing files for shape)
2. Run `npm run sync:contentful`

**To run the sync:**

```
npm run sync:contentful
```

Requires `CONTENTFUL_MANAGEMENT_TOKEN` — a personal token tied to your own Contentful account — in `.env.shared` (never commit; run `npm run env -- init` to scaffold it, then `npm run env -- <tier>` to activate a tier before running the sync). Get the token from `app.contentful.com/account/profile/cma_tokens`. `CONTENTFUL_SPACE_ID` is shared across tiers; `CONTENTFUL_ENVIRONMENT_ID` is set per tier and auto-fetched by `npm run env -- init` once the management token is filled in.

The script is idempotent — safe to re-run. It preserves any existing fields not in the definition file (it will not delete fields from a live content type).

**Relationship to the React component:**
Each content type definition in `scripts/contentful/content-types/` corresponds to a React component in `overrides/app/components/contentful/`. The content type's field IDs must match the TypeScript type in `overrides/app/types/contentful.ts`.

**Experience Builder components** (drag-and-drop in Contentful Studio) are a separate concern — they are registered in `overrides/app/components/contentful/experiences/definitions.ts` and do not need a corresponding `sync:contentful` entry unless they also have a standard content type for use outside Studio.

## Integration Map

All order-creation, fulfilment write, and CRM sync traffic from SFCC routes through MuleSoft as the middleware layer — SFCC does not call NewStore, AP21, Omneo, or Narvar directly. In addition, the PWA's MRT Node layer calls MuleSoft directly for read operations (order history, order details, boutique / BOPIS stock check, real-time stock availability, GiveX balance check) — SFCC is not in those read paths. A handful of services are also called **browser-direct from the PWA** and another set are **SFCC cartridge integrations** invoked server-side. The `Boundary` column makes this explicit so you know where to look when an integration breaks.

**Boundary key:**

- **PWA-direct** — called from the browser directly. Vendor key (if any) is publishable/public and safe in the bundle.
- **MRT-mediated** — called from the PWA's Node layer via `/mobify/proxy/` or a server-only endpoint. API credentials held as MRT environment variables; never reach the browser bundle. Includes direct PWA → MuleSoft calls via MRT proxy.

- **SFCC (cartridge)** — vendor-supplied or custom server-side cartridge running inside SFCC.
- **SFCC → MuleSoft** — SFCC calls MuleSoft, which fans out to the downstream system.
- **Browser handoff** — PWA hands the user off to a third party's hosted experience.
- **Out-of-band** — no runtime call from PWA or SFCC; the integration delivers data via a separate channel.

## Cross-Storefront Session & Basket Scope

All eight storefronts are path-prefixed on a single first-party domain and share one SFCC realm with shared customer data. The `httpOnly` SLAS refresh-token cookie set by the SSR layer is therefore presented on every storefront prefix — no cross-domain SSO bridge is needed. SLAS tokens are channel-scoped, so the SSR layer re-initialises the SLAS context per storefront; a registered shopper is silently re-recognised across a storefront switch (shared customer record), while a guest session is site-scoped and does not carry over. **The basket deliberately does not transfer across storefronts** — baskets are site-scoped and priced in the storefront's own currency/pricebook, so a shopper switching storefront starts a fresh basket. Carrying a basket across a currency boundary would produce incorrect pricing. The Global-e checkout handoff is a separate session boundary (Global-e owns its hosted checkout in full). The exact SLAS re-authorisation mechanism and the stay-signed-in UX are open items with the Salesforce integration team.

## Blast-Radius Mitigation

Multiple upstream integrations (SFCC, MuleSoft/Omneo, Global-e, Narvar, Contentful, Didomi, Inside Chat) mean a failure or attack targeting one service must not cascade. A PWA-relevant mitigation can be done in the SSR layer.

The SSR layer in `overrides/app/ssr.js` uses **Node's native `fetch`**, which is backed by `undici`. Undici's `dispatcher` option (the per-call `dispatcher` option on individual `fetch()` invocations) allows each upstream origin to be given its own connection pool with an independent cap. This prevents a slow or flooded integration (e.g. checkout APIs) from exhausting connections for unrelated origins (e.g. Contentful, JWKS).

```ts
import { Pool } from 'undici';

// 1. Create isolated pools for specific origins
const checkoutPool = new Pool('https://api.checkout-service.com', {
  connections: 10, // Hard limit of 10 concurrent connections to this origin
  timeout: 8000,
});

// 2. Use them explicitly in your fetch calls inside ssr.js
async function getCheckoutMetadata() {
  return await fetch('https://api.checkout-service.com/v1/metadata', {
    dispatcher: checkoutPool, // Safely isolated!
  });
}
```

> **Scope.** PWA-layer only (browser-direct and MRT-proxied). Backend integrations consumed by SFCC via MuleSoft (NewStore writes, AP21 — including the inbound product + pricing feed, Omneo profile sync, Emarsys, Narvar back office, Avalara, GiveX validate / redeem / refund, Transperfect) are addressed by the SFCC ↔ MuleSoft middleware design and are not duplicated here.

The documents are grouped by role rather than by runtime load order. A reader new to the system can start at the top and build a mental model from the most central systems outwards.

The FED Lead is pushing back on the microservices argument by pointing out that the codebase already isolates connections per origin through undici pools, so I need to clarify what that isolation actually covers versus where genuine single points of failure still exist in a monolithic architecture.

The per-origin connection pools protect against head-of-line blocking at the HTTP client level — if one upstream service gets slow, it won't starve connections meant for other services — and they enforce timeout bounds so hung upstreams release quickly. But this is connection-level isolation, not application-level isolation.

The real vulnerability is that everything still runs in a single Node process with a shared event loop and heap. If one integration's code does heavy synchronous work — parsing a massive JSON payload, running expensive crypto, or transforming a large response — it blocks the entire event loop and stalls every other request on that Lambda instance. Similarly, a memory leak or huge response buffer from one integration can OOM the whole worker and crash all in-flight requests. Connection pool isolation doesn't help with either of these failure modes because the CPU and memory are fundamentally shared.

Beyond runtime failures, there's the deployment problem: one app means one bundle and one deploy cycle, so a fix for one integration forces a redeploy of the entire storefront including checkout, and you can't release or rollback integrations independently. The larger bundle also hurts cold starts on Lambda. Separate apps would give each integration its own process, memory ceiling, and release cadence.

There's also the security angle — all integration credentials live as environment variables in a single process, so a compromise or logging mistake in one integration's code path exposes every other integration's secrets. And scaling becomes coupled too: all integrations scale together with storefront traffic rather than independently.

That said, the connection pool isolation does address the most naive version of the single-point-of-failure concern about socket starvation, so it's not a complete invalidation of the microservices approach.

The real question sharpens then: connection pools isolate network resources, but they don't isolate compute, memory, process lifecycle, deploy cadence, or security blast radius. Those remaining shared-fate dimensions are what physical process separation actually buys. So the spike needs to reframe the SPOF discussion as "how much isolation, at what layer, is worth the operational cost?" rather than just "isolated or not" — in-process pooling is the cheap 80% solution.

For MRT specifically, there's a nuance worth highlighting: each request lands on a different Lambda instance, so a single crashing request doesn't take down "the server" the way it would on a traditional always-on Node process. That actually weakens some of the crash-blast-radius argument compared to a long-lived server model, which is an important MRT-specific consideration.

But event-loop blocking and memory pressure still affect concurrent requests on the same warm instance, and deploy-coupling remains entirely unaffected by Lambda's per-request isolation. I need to be precise about MRT's execution model here — whether the PWA Kit Express server on MRT handles one request per instance at a time or multiple concurrent requests on a single warm instance actually matters for the event-loop argument, so I should verify that detail.

Great question — and you've put your finger on exactly the thing the TSD has to get right, because the naive version of the SPOF argument is *already wrong* for this codebase.

## Yes, it has isolation — but only at one layer

What `connectionPools.ts` gives you is **network-resource isolation**. Each upstream (SCAPI, MuleSoft, Marketing Cloud, Booxi…) gets its own `undici` pool with a hard connection cap and its own timeouts. The specific failure it kills is **socket starvation / head-of-line blocking**: without it, one slow upstream (say MuleSoft hanging) could consume every outbound socket in the shared agent and starve unrelated calls to Contentful or SCAPI. With per-origin pools, a flooded MuleSoft can only exhaust *its own* 20 connections; everything else keeps flowing.

That is real, and it genuinely neutralises the **weakest** form of "single app = single point of failure." If someone's argument for splitting is *only* "a slow integration will hang the whole site," that's already answered — in-process, for free, no microservices needed.

## But that's one failure mode out of several

Connection pools isolate **sockets**. They do nothing for everything else the one process shares. Here's the honest layer-by-layer picture:

| Shared-fate dimension | Single app + pools? | Separate MRT apps? |
|---|---|---|
| **Socket / connection exhaustion** | ✅ Isolated (pools) | ✅ Isolated |
| **CPU / event loop** (one integration does heavy sync work → blocks *everyone's* render) | ❌ Shared | ✅ Isolated |
| **Heap / OOM** (leak or huge payload in one integration kills the worker) | ❌ Shared | ✅ Isolated |
| **Process crash** (unhandled rejection on one code path) | ❌ Shared | ✅ Isolated |
| **Deploy / release cadence** (fix Booxi → redeploy checkout too; no independent rollback) | ❌ Shared | ✅ Isolated |
| **Bundle size / cold start** (all integration code in one bundle, worse LCP) | ❌ Shared | ✅ Isolated |
| **Secret blast radius** (every integration's credentials live in one process' env) | ❌ Shared | ✅ Compartmentalised |
| **Independent scaling** (webhook receiver scales with storefront traffic, can't decouple) | ❌ Shared | ✅ Isolated |

The pools protect the **plumbing**. They don't protect the **compute, the memory, the process lifecycle, the deploy pipeline, or the secret store** — and *those* are what physical app separation buys.

## The two weak points that survive everything

Two of those rows have nothing to do with runtime isolation at all, so no amount of clever in-process engineering closes them:

1. **Deploy coupling.** One app = one bundle = one deploy. Squad A's change and Squad B's change ship together; you can't roll back one integration without rolling back the storefront. This is arguably the *strongest* Option B argument and connection pools don't touch it.
2. **Secret compartmentalisation.** A logging mistake or a compromise on the Vimeo code path sits in the same process that holds the MuleSoft and Marketing Cloud credentials. Separate apps = separate secret scopes.

## One MRT-specific nuance the spike must confirm (don't assert it)

MRT is serverless — the SSR runs as a function behind CloudFront, and requests spread across instances. That already gives you *some* per-invocation isolation a traditional always-on Node box wouldn't: a single crashing request doesn't take down "the server," it takes down that invocation. **This actually weakens the crash/OOM blast-radius argument** — but only partially, because event-loop blocking and memory pressure still hit *concurrent* requests on the same warm instance. **The exact per-instance concurrency model is the thing to verify in the spike**, because it directly determines how much the CPU/memory rows above actually bite. I won't state it as fact here — it's a "confirm with the platform team" item, exactly the kind SFCC-122 routed to Victor.

## So, to your three questions directly

- **Does the single app have isolation?** Yes — but one kind (network), not all kinds.
- **Does that invalidate microservices?** No. It invalidates the *weakest* argument for them ("no isolation"), while leaving the strong ones (compute/memory/process fate-sharing, deploy coupling, secret blast radius) fully intact.
- **Is there a weak point the microservices approach handles?** Yes — several, but the two that can't be engineered away in a single app are **independent deploy/rollback** and **secret compartmentalisation**.

## What this changes for the spike

It reframes the whole SPOF axis from **binary to a spectrum**:

> It's not "isolated vs not isolated." It's *"how much isolation, at which layer, is worth how much operational cost?"*

In-process pooling is the cheap 80% and it's already done. Separate apps are the expensive remaining 20% (process + deploy + secret isolation) that you pay for in N× environments, N× deploys, and N× ops overhead. So the recommendation shouldn't rest on "microservices are safer" — it should hinge on a concrete question:

**Is any single integration critical *and* volatile enough** — e.g. payment metadata, or a checkout-adjacent proxy — **that independent deploy/rollback and secret isolation justify pulling *that one* out**, while the long tail stays in the modular monolith?

That points naturally at **Option C** (one app, cleanly modular inside — where the code already sits) as the baseline, with Option B applied *surgically* rather than wholesale. That's a far stronger TSD conclusion than a blanket A-or-B, and it's exactly the kind of nuance the connection-pool detail forces you toward.
